description: Tracing an 'oc'/'kubectl' request to the hosted cluster's API. It enters the management cluster through the Shared Ingress proxy's MetalLB VIP, is SNI-routed by hostname to this guest's kube-apiserver Service, and terminates at the Guest API Server Pod in the HCP namespace. This control-plane path stays entirely in the management cluster and never enters a guest worker VM. The OAuth, Konnectivity, and Ignition endpoints ride the same shared ingress.

steps.description: An 'oc' client resolves the guest's API hostname (api.<guest>) to the Shared Ingress LoadBalancer VIP. With no cloud LB present, a MetalLB speaker answers ARP for the VIP, so the request lands on the bare metal cluster.

The LoadBalancer Service DNATs the VIP to a healthy Shared Ingress Proxy endpoint. HAProxy reads the TLS SNI hostname and selects this hosted cluster's control-plane backend (the same proxy fronts OAuth, Konnectivity, and Ignition by hostname too).

The proxy forwards the connection to this guest's kube-apiserver Service in the HCP namespace. The Guest API Server Pod terminates the request, authenticates it, and serves it from etcd — the traffic never leaves the management control plane.

description: Tracing an inbound HTTPS request to a guest application on the *.apps wildcard domain. Unlike API traffic, this never touches the Shared Ingress Proxy: it enters through the Apps Ingress LoadBalancer (the infra-side Service the kubevirt cloud provider mirrors from the guest's router-default LB, advertised by MetalLB), crosses into the KubeVirt VM, and is handled by the guest cluster's own OpenShift Ingress Router before reaching the front-end ClusterIP Service and Pod.

steps.description: The client resolves an app hostname under *.apps.<guest-domain> to the Apps Ingress LoadBalancer VIP. This infra-side LoadBalancer — created by the kubevirt cloud provider to back the guest's router-default Service — is advertised by a MetalLB speaker, so the packet lands on the bare metal cluster. The control-plane Shared Ingress Proxy is not involved.

The LoadBalancer Service DNATs the VIP to a virt-launcher endpoint, and the packet enters the bare metal worker node's OVS br-int bridge, which applies OVN flow rules to route it toward the KubeVirt Launcher hosting the guest router's node.
OVS routes the packet through the tap0 virtual interface into the KubeVirt Launcher Pod, crossing the host-to-VM network boundary.
The KubeVirt Launcher delivers the packet to the virtio-net NIC of the Guest Worker Node VM, shifting context from the host kernel to the guest RHCOS kernel.
The guest RHCOS kernel hands the packet to the in-VM Open vSwitch service, which evaluates guest OVN flow rules for the router-default Service.
Guest OVS matches the router-default LoadBalancer (the guest-side half of this path, whose external IP the kubevirt CCM wired to the infra VIP) and applies its OVN load-balancer flow.
The Service DNATs to an OpenShift Ingress Router Pod inside the VM, which terminates TLS and matches the request against its Route table for the *.apps hostname.
The guest Ingress Router forwards the request to the Front-End Service — the ClusterIP that fronts the frontend Pods — addressing its stable virtual IP rather than a Pod directly.
OVN load-balancer flows DNAT the ClusterIP to a ready Front-End Application Pod endpoint. The application process accepts the connection and returns a response.

description: Tracing how a new application Pod is scheduled and started in the guest cluster: from a kubectl apply hitting the Guest API Server through scheduling, kubelet notification, and CRI-O container creation inside the Guest VM.

steps.description: Developer runs 'oc apply -f deployment.yaml'. The request reaches the Guest API Server, which validates it, persists the Deployment to etcd, and notifies controllers via watch events.
The Guest Scheduler watches for Pods with no node assignment. It evaluates guest worker node capacity and affinity rules, then selects the Guest Worker Node VM.
The Scheduler writes a Binding object back to the Guest API Server, officially assigning the Pod to the Guest Worker Node.

The guest kubelet maintains its own outbound watch on the Guest API Server (via the exposed apiserver endpoint) and observes the newly bound Pod assigned to its node. The kubelet pulls its application over that same outbound watch — the API Server never pushes the assignment to it. (Konnectivity is not involved here; that tunnel only carries API-Server-initiated traffic such as exec/logs/port-forward.)

Kubelet validates the spec and issues RunPodSandbox and CreateContainer gRPC calls to guest CRI-O, which pulls the image, sets up the cgroup hierarchy, and invokes the CNI plugin to provision the Pod's network namespace.
Guest CRI-O starts the container via runc. The application process becomes PID 1 inside its namespaces, registers with the guest network, and the Pod transitions to Running status.

description: Tracing an in-cluster call from the Front-End Application to the Back-End Application through the Back-End ClusterIP Service: name resolution to a virtual IP, OVN load-balancer DNAT on the guest OVS fabric, a NetworkPolicy ACL check, and delivery to a backing Pod — no ingress, no traffic leaving the VM.

steps.description: The Front-End resolves backend.e-commerce-prod.svc.cluster.local to the Back-End Service's ClusterIP and opens a connection to that stable virtual IP rather than to a specific backend Pod.

The connection to the ClusterIP enters the in-VM OVS br-int bridge, where the OVN-Kubernetes load-balancer flow installed for this Service matches the virtual IP and selects a healthy backend endpoint.

Before the packet is delivered, the OVN logical pipeline on br-int evaluates the NetworkPolicy ACLs compiled for the backend port group. The policy admits the Front-End Pods' address set as an allowed ingress source, so the connection passes the ACL gate (traffic from any other source would be dropped here).

With the policy allowing the flow, OVS DNATs the destination from the ClusterIP to the chosen Back-End Application Pod IP and delivers the packet over its veth pair. The backend process accepts the connection and returns its response.

description: Tracing how a new Hosted Control Plane and its first KubeVirt worker come up: the HyperShift Operator reconciles the HostedCluster, the per-HCP control-plane-operator brings up etcd and the Guest API Server, and the NodePool is turned into a VirtualMachineInstance via Cluster API and the KubeVirt provider.

steps.description: Platform admin applies a HostedCluster and a NodePool manifest via 'oc apply'. These CRs live in the management (bare metal) cluster, so the Management Kube API Server persists them and notifies the HyperShift Operator.

The HyperShift Operator (a cluster-wide singleton in the 'hypershift' namespace) reconciles the HostedCluster CR: it creates the dedicated HCP namespace and deploys the per-HCP control-plane-operator into it.

The control-plane-operator becomes the per-hosted-cluster owner of the guest control plane, reconciling each control-plane component (etcd, Guest API Server, OAuth, Konnectivity, Ignition) inside the HCP namespace.
The control-plane-operator deploys the etcd StatefulSet. Once etcd reaches quorum it brings up the Guest API Server, OAuth Server, Konnectivity Server, and Ignition Server as Deployments.

In parallel, the HyperShift Operator reconciles the NodePool into Cluster API objects (Cluster, MachineDeployment). The cluster-api-provider-kubevirt (CAPK) running in the HCP namespace requests a KubeVirt VirtualMachine for each desired replica.

CAPK creates a VirtualMachine object; KubeVirt's virt-controller creates the virt-launcher Pod for it, and virt-handler on the bare metal worker node then signals that Pod to start the qemu-kvm process and boot the RHCOS VirtualMachineInstance.
As RHCOS boots, the VM fetches its Ignition config from the Ignition Server over TLS. The payload carries the kubelet bootstrap certificates and machine config needed to join the guest cluster.

Inside the VM the Konnectivity Agent dials out to the Konnectivity Server, and the guest kubelet registers the node with the Guest API Server. The worker goes Ready and the hosted cluster can schedule applications.

description: Tracing how raising a NodePool's replica count becomes a brand-new RHCOS worker VM: the HyperShift NodePool controller renders it into Cluster API, CAPK turns the desired Machine into a KubeVirt VirtualMachine, and virt-handler boots the VMI until it registers as a guest node.

steps.description: A platform admin runs 'oc scale nodepool <name> --replicas=N+1'. The NodePool lives in the management cluster, so the Management Kube API Server persists the higher desired replica count.
The HyperShift Operator's NodePool controller observes that desired replicas now exceed the running workers and renders the NodePool into updated Cluster API objects (MachineDeployment / MachineSet).
The Cluster API Manager reconciles the scaled MachineSet by creating one new Machine object to represent the additional worker.
Cluster API delegates infrastructure creation for the new Machine to the cluster-api-provider-kubevirt (CAPK).
CAPK creates a KubeVirt VirtualMachine; KubeVirt's virt-controller creates the virt-launcher Pod for the resulting VMI, which the management scheduler places on a bare metal worker.
virt-handler on that bare metal node signals the launcher Pod's libvirt to boot the qemu-kvm domain (it drives the boot on the node; it does not create the Pod).
The launcher starts the RHCOS VirtualMachineInstance for the new worker.
As it boots, the VM fetches its Ignition config over TLS, receiving the kubelet bootstrap credentials and machine config needed to join the guest cluster.
The new node's kubelet registers with the Guest API Server and goes Ready; the NodePool's desired replica count is now satisfied.

description: Tracing the reverse path: lowering a NodePool's replicas walks back down the Cluster API chain so CAPK deletes a KubeVirt VirtualMachine and the worker VM is drained and shut down.

steps.description: The admin scales the NodePool down. The Management Kube API Server records the lower desired replica count.
The HyperShift Operator's NodePool controller sees more workers running than desired and scales the MachineDeployment down.
The Cluster API Manager selects a Machine to remove and marks it for deletion.
Cluster API asks the KubeVirt provider to delete the VirtualMachine backing that Machine.
Deleting the VirtualMachine makes virt-controller terminate the virt-launcher Pod for that VMI.
The launcher gracefully shuts the RHCOS VMI down; the qemu-kvm process exits and the tap0 NIC is torn down.
The node is cordoned, drained, and deleted from the guest cluster; the NodePool now matches its desired size.

description: Tracing an 'oc exec' from a developer to a process inside a guest application Pod. Because the Guest API Server cannot route to the node network directly, the call rides the API-Server-initiated Konnectivity tunnel down to the node's kubelet and CRI-O.

steps.description: A developer runs 'oc exec -it <pod> -- sh'. The request authenticates against the Guest API Server, which must reach the kubelet on the node hosting the Pod.
The Guest API Server cannot dial the guest node network directly, so it hands the exec stream to the Konnectivity Server — the one direction the tunnel carries (API-Server-initiated traffic).
The server proxies the call through the persistent tunnel to the Konnectivity Agent running inside the target worker VM.
The agent forwards the request to the guest kubelet on that node.
The kubelet issues an Exec CRI call to guest CRI-O for the target container.
CRI-O enters the container's namespaces and runs the command; stdout/stderr stream back up the same tunnel to the developer's terminal.

description: Tracing how a application Pod turns a Service name into a ClusterIP: the Pod's stub resolver queries the node-local CoreDNS, which answers from the guest cluster's Service records before the caller opens the real connection.

steps.description: The Front-End looks up 'backend.e-commerce-prod.svc.cluster.local'. Its /etc/resolv.conf points at the cluster DNS, so the query goes to the node-local CoreDNS Pod.
CoreDNS resolves cluster-local names from the Service and EndpointSlice records it syncs from the Guest API Server (external names would instead be forwarded to the upstream resolvers).
CoreDNS returns the Back-End Service's ClusterIP to the caller and caches the record for subsequent lookups.
With the name resolved, the Front-End opens its connection to the Back-End ClusterIP — where the east-west Service flow takes over.

description: A guest worker VM dies unexpectedly. virt-handler reports the loss and the NodePool → Cluster API → KubeVirt chain — the closer — detects that observed replicas no longer match desired and rebuilds the VM until the worker is healthy again.

steps.description: The RHCOS VMI's qemu-kvm process dies. virt-handler on the bare metal node detects that the libvirt domain has stopped.
virt-handler updates the VirtualMachineInstance's status to Failed on the Management Kube API Server.
The KubeVirt provider sees its KubevirtMachine has lost its VMI — observed state no longer matches the desired Machine.
CAPK reports the Machine as failed up to Cluster API, which now has fewer ready replicas than the MachineSet wants.
The shortfall surfaces to the NodePool controller: the NodePool's desired replica count is no longer met.
Closing the loop, the NodePool controller drives Cluster API to create a replacement Machine to restore the desired count.
Cluster API asks CAPK for a fresh VirtualMachine to back the new Machine.
virt-controller creates a new virt-launcher Pod for the replacement VMI, scheduled onto a healthy bare metal worker.
virt-handler boots the replacement RHCOS VMI; the worker rejoins the guest cluster and desired state is restored.

description: Resource pressure on a bare metal worker evicts a virt-launcher Pod, killing its VM. The reconcile loop notices the VMI lost its Pod and reschedules a fresh launcher onto a node with capacity — closing the gap between desired and observed.

steps.description: Under memory/CPU pressure the host kubelet evicts the virt-launcher Pod; its qemu-kvm process is killed and the VM goes down.
The kubelet reports the launcher Pod as Evicted/Failed to the Management Kube API Server.
virt-handler sees the VMI it was managing has lost its launcher Pod and marks the instance's observed state accordingly.
The degraded VMI surfaces to the KubeVirt provider, whose backing Machine no longer matches the desired running state.
Reconciling toward desired state, virt-controller creates a fresh virt-launcher Pod for the VMI.
The management scheduler binds the replacement launcher Pod to a bare metal worker that has capacity (avoiding the pressured node).
virt-handler on the new node boots the VMI again; the worker rejoins the guest cluster.

description: A hosted control-plane Pod — the Guest API Server — crashes. Because it is a Deployment managed in the management cluster, the management control loops recreate it: the guest cluster's brain is self-healing without operator intervention.

steps.description: The Guest API Server Pod process crashes. The bare metal kubelet running it records the container as exited.
The kubelet reports the Pod's failed status to the Management Kube API Server.
The ReplicaSet controller sees one fewer ready replica than the Guest API Server Deployment desires — a gap to reconcile.
Closing the loop, it creates a replacement Pod to satisfy the ReplicaSet's desired count.
The new Pod is unscheduled; the management scheduler evaluates bare metal node capacity.
The scheduler writes a Binding placing the replacement Pod on a healthy node.
The chosen node's kubelet is notified and starts the replacement Guest API Server container via CRI-O.
The Guest API Server comes back up and resumes serving; the hosted control plane is healthy again.

eventName: ConfigMap Update → Live in a Pod
description: Tracing what really happens after 'oc apply -f configmap.yaml'. There is NO bespoke operator that rolls a plain ConfigMap edit into a running Pod: the apply only rewrites the ConfigMap record in guest etcd. Volume-mounted ConfigMaps are refreshed in place by the guest kubelet (but the app must re-read the file), while env-var and subPath consumers see nothing until the Pod is recreated. To make the new config actually live you change the desired Pod state — 'oc rollout restart' (or a config-hash annotation) bumps the Deployment's pod template, and the Deployment controller inside the Guest Controller Manager then rolls a fresh Pod that reads the updated ConfigMap at startup. (A tool like Stakater Reloader can watch ConfigMaps/Secrets and fire that rollout restart automatically — the closest thing to an operator that does this for you.)

steps.description: A developer edits the ConfigMap and runs 'oc apply -f configmap.yaml' against the hosted cluster. The Guest API Server validates the object and increments its resourceVersion — but updating a ConfigMap does not, by itself, touch any Pod or Deployment.

The API Server persists the new ConfigMap revision to guest etcd. This is the ONLY change a bare ConfigMap update makes: the Guest Controller Manager runs no loop that restarts workloads on a plain ConfigMap edit, so this write by itself leaves every running Pod untouched.

For Pods that mount the ConfigMap as a VOLUME, the guest kubelet's configmap-and-secret manager notices the changed object on its next sync (~1 min + cache TTL) and atomically swaps the projected files in the Pod's volume. The container now sees new file contents — but the application process must re-read them itself (a file watcher or SIGHUP). If it's a volume mount AND the app watches the file, this is the whole story: the config is live with no rollout. Otherwise — a process that loaded config only at startup, and every env-var or subPath consumer — still runs the OLD values.

To force the new config live (the only option for env-var / subPath consumers, and the clean option for everyone else), the developer mutates the workload's DESIRED state: 'oc rollout restart deployment/<app>' — or bumping a checksum/config-hash annotation on the pod template. This patch to the Deployment is the actual desired-state change the question is about. A rollout is often preferred even when hot-reload would work: it converges every replica atomically (instead of each kubelet's independent ~1-min timer), it is gated by readiness probes so a bad config halts the rollout with old Pods still serving, and it leaves a revision you can 'rollout undo'.

The Deployment controller (a reconcile loop inside the Guest Controller Manager — not a standalone operator) sees the pod-template hash changed and creates a new ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet controller then rolls that new ReplicaSet out, bringing its replicas up while retiring the old ones per the rollout strategy.

The controllers write the new ReplicaSet and its Pod objects back to the API Server. The freshly desired Pods reference the updated pod template, so when they start they will pull the current ConfigMap revision from step 2.
The new Pod has no node assignment, so the Guest Scheduler evaluates guest worker capacity and affinity and selects a Guest Worker Node VM for it.
The Scheduler writes a Binding back to the Guest API Server, assigning the replacement Pod to the chosen guest worker node.
The guest kubelet observes the newly bound Pod on its own outbound watch of the Guest API Server (not via the Konnectivity tunnel, which only carries API-Server-initiated traffic such as exec/logs).

Kubelet issues RunPodSandbox / CreateContainer calls to guest CRI-O. CRI-O mounts the ConfigMap volume and injects any ConfigMap-sourced env vars from the CURRENT revision, so the new container is built around the updated config.

CRI-O starts the container via runc; the application reads the updated ConfigMap at startup and goes Running with the new config live. Once it is Ready the old Pod is terminated and the rollout is complete.
